title: Seasonal constellations

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 25 Nov 2026 against Royal Museums Greenwich night-sky guides (Orion a winter constellation, Leo spring, the Summer Triangle and Scorpius summer, the Square of Pegasus autumn; the Plough and Cassiopeia circumpolar from the UK), NASA Space Place on why the night sky changes with Earth's orbit, and NGSS 5-ESS1-2. The lab computes rather than asserts: constellation directions use real right ascensions (Orion 5.5 h, Leo 10.7 h, Scorpius 16.9 h, Pegasus 23.0 h) and the midnight direction is 7.7 h + 2 h per month, so Orion is opposite the Sun in December and lost in daylight May to July, Leo is behind the Sun in August-September, Scorpius in November-December. Orion's due-south time (about 10 pm mid-January, 2 h earlier per month) matches a sidereal day of 23 h 56 min. The adult text states the model shows midnight, that evening visibility lags a month or two, that times are for Britain without summer time, that Scorpius is low from Britain, and that circumpolar status depends on latitude.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips reported by Plummer (2009) and Sharp (1996) on children's astronomy: stars switch off or leave in summer (step 1 and 2 predictions, the 'off' slip, the hidden-by-daylight task); constellations move round space (the 'move' slip; the star patterns never change in the lab, only Earth moves); clouds or Earth's tilt causing it ('cloud' and 'tilt' slips, the adult text separates tilt from orbit); stars rising at the same time every night (step 4 prediction and the 'time' slip); every constellation being seasonal (step 5 prediction about the Plough, the 'set' slip); the Southern Hemisphere sharing northern seasons ('south' slip, mastery m6).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is this topic's own: a top-down orbit where Earth's month sets the night side's midnight direction against four constellations placed by right ascension, with a computed visibility class (high, part of the night, lost in daylight); a 9 pm south-facing horizon view where Orion's hour angle shifts 2 hours per month; and a north-facing view where the Plough and Cassiopeia rotate round Polaris by season with pointers kept aimed at the North Star. It is not flagplough (finding the Plough and Polaris on one night, ages 5-7) or flagmoonorbit (Moon phases); the gate measured under 30% source overlap with every flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: Every rule is met by acting before it is stated: dragging Earth round turns the dashed night-side line and the 'night side at midnight' window from Orion to Leo to Scorpius to Pegasus; in June the learner has to look past the Sun to find Orion, and a wrong tap explains whether that pattern is high or only up for part of the night; the season sort refuses wrong boxes with the reason from the same model; stepping month buttons slides Orion from the eastern horizon through due south to the west while the clock time for due south drops 2 hours per month; switching seasons turns the Plough round the North Star while it stays above the horizon.

predictions.evidence: Four committed predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'Why is Orion easy to see in winter but not in summer?' (its stars switch off, or clouds); 'In June, where are the stars of Orion?' (gone from space, or moved to the other side of the Sun); 'Orion is due south at 10 pm in January; where is it at 10 pm a month later?' (in the same place); 'From Britain, can you see the Plough on summer nights?' (no, it is a winter constellation). Tasks cannot complete until a prediction is locked, and the done message names the learner's prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions; every wrong option is tagged with its own slip message: 'off' (stars never switch off, they are in the day sky), 'cloud' (clouds come and go, Orion is near the Sun), 'move' (the stars stay put, Earth moves), 'tilt' (tilt gives hot and cold seasons, the orbit sets which stars fill the night), 'season' (Orion winter, Leo spring, Scorpius summer, Pegasus autumn), 'time' (4 minutes a night, 2 hours a month), 'set' (circumpolar patterns never set from Britain), 'south' (December is summer in the south and Orion is upside down).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences, name one idea each and define constellation, night side and set in plain words; validate_lessons.py passed both readability limits after the adult text was rewritten into shorter sentences. Lab strips are one to three lines on a 390 px phone, buttons are one or two words ('1 month', 'Winter', 'All year: Leo'), and month names are written out on the orbit.

no_filler.evidence: The four kid paragraphs teach: what a constellation is; why the night side changes direction; the four seasonal patterns and why a missing one is in the day sky; 4 minutes a night and the circumpolar exception. Adult paragraphs give the standards and key words, the precise model with its stated simplifications, the named mistakes, and what each lab step does. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in dark and light themes for every step after Show me: the space view and the night-side window stack vertically with the month label and all four constellation names inside the panel; the season boxes sit in a 2 by 2 grid; the 9 pm view keeps East, South and West readable on the grass band with eight month tabs in one row; the north view's labels were moved so Cassiopeia and the Plough never clip the panel edge or collide with compass labels; the six answer cards fit in two rows of three.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label (Back one month, Forward one month, Forward three months, '<Name> is in the day sky in June', '<Name> is high on winter nights', One month earlier or later, 'Show the northern sky on a summer evening', '<Name> can be seen all year'). The canvas aria-label updates with every message, challenge feedback is a polite live region, and walk.cjs ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations.
